AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: The association between hyperuricemia and stroke outcome still remains controversial worldwide. This study aims to determine the prevalence of hyperuricemia and its association with the outcome of patients with acute ischemic stroke in a tertiary care hospital.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: This was a hospital-based prospective cohort study that included patients with ischemic stroke with baseline uric acid levels and 3-month post-stroke follow-up data. Associations between hyperuricemia and stroke outcomes were analyzed using multiple logistic regression, Kaplan-Meier, and Cox proportional hazards regression analysis.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: A total of 480 patients were reviewed with a mean age of 62.8 ± 13.3 years. The prevalence of hyperuricemia was 52.3% with mean uricemia of 71.1 ± 25.3 mg/dL. There was a significant association between hyperuricemia and mortality with unadjusted odds ratio (OR) = 4.120 [95% (confidence interval [CI]: 2.466-7.153); P = .001)], but on multivariate analysis, hyperuricemia was not an independent predictor of stroke mortality [OR = 1.270 (CI: .547-2.946); P = .578)]. An independent association between increasing uric acid levels and mortality was noted on Cox proportional hazards regression; adjusted hazard ratio (95% CI) of 3.395 (2.114-5.452), P value greater than .001. Stroke mortality significantly increased across higher uric acid quintiles in patients with acute stroke (P < .001). Hyperuricemia was an independent predictor of poor functional outcome within 3 months after stroke with adjusted OR (95% CI) of 2.820 (1.359-5.851); P = .005.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Half of black African patients with ischemic stroke present with hyperuricemia, and hyperuricemia is a predictor of mortality and adverse functional outcomes. Further studies are therefore warranted to determine whether reducing hyperuricemia after stroke would be beneficial within our setting.
